raw.abstractText:
Background

Tibial transverse osteotomy (TTO) is a promising but limited surgical option for diabetic foot (DF). Berberine, a natural compound from Coptis chinensis, exhibits anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic effects relevant to metabolic diseases.

Objectives

This study aimed to evaluate whether adjunctive berberine enhances the therapeutic outcomes of TTO in DF patients and to explore its potential association with the platelet-derived growth factor-B (PDGF-B)/PDGF receptor-β (PDGFRβ) signaling pathway.

Methods

This was a prospective, single-center, randomized, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, blinded trial. Of 200 screened DF patients, 96 eligible participants (Wagner grade 2-4) scheduled for TTO were randomized 1:1 to receive either TTO plus local berberine injections (n=48) or TTO plus local saline placebo (n=48). An additional non-randomized diabetic reference group (n=10) and healthy control group (n=10) were included for exploratory cellular studies only. The primary outcome was the total effective rate of ulcer healing at 3 months. Secondary outcomes included changes in Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI), ulcer area, Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain score and serum inflammatory markers (hs-CRP, IL-6). Exploratory outcomes comprised serum VEGF, bFGF and PDGF-B levels, as well as fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue.

Results

All 96 randomized participants completed the 3-month follow-up, with no dropouts. The berberine group demonstrated a significantly higher total effective rate than the surgery-alone group (87.5% vs. 68.8%; risk difference, 18.7%; 95% CI, 1.2% to 36.2%; P < 0.05). At 3 months, the berberine group also showed greater improvements in ABI (mean difference, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.08 to 0.18; P < 0.01) and ulcer healing rate (mean difference, 16.7%; 95% CI, 9.5% to 23.9%; P < 0.01), along with more significant reductions in hs-CRP and IL-6. Berberine treatment was associated with reduced fibroblast apoptosis in wound tissue (mean difference, -1.10%; 95% CI, -1.56% to -0.64%; P = 0.001) and lower protein expression of PDGF-B and PDGFRβ. No severe adverse events related to berberine injections were reported.

Conclusion

In DF patients undergoing TTO, adjunctive local berberine therapy significantly improves the total effective rate and promotes ulcer healing, with benefits associated with reduced inflammation and fibroblast apoptosis and downregulation of the PDGF-B/PDGFRβ pathway. These findings are correlative and require further mechanistic validation. Larger multi-center trials are needed to confirm efficacy and safety.

raw.abstractText: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent the first line of host immune defense against a broad spectrum of microorganisms. Whether naturally occurring or synthetically designed, these small peptides can potently inhibit microbial growth and remain stable under diverse conditions. Most AMPs act by directly disrupting fungal or bacterial membranes. In this study, we identified a glycine-rich peptide with strong antifungal activity against Botrytis cinerea. We further investigated its mode of action (MOA) and demonstrated its preventive antifungal activity in plants. Our work focuses primarily on the in vitro characterization of AMP features in the context of plant-Botrytis interactions.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Liver fibrosis is a chronic wound healing process of liver injury and gut-liver axis dysregulation has been recently identified as an important contributor to liver fibrosis progression. Quercetin has been reported to have anti-inflammatory activity and microbiota-modulating effects. However, the potential targets of quercetin remain unclear, as does the relationship between quercetin-associated targets and changes in the gut microbiota in liver fibrosis.

Objectives

The purpose of this study was to use network pharmacology to predict potential targets of quercetin associated with liver fibrosis and to explore changes in gut microbiota following treatment with quercetin using a CCl4-induced rat model.

Methods

Eighteen male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomized into CON group, MOD group and QR group (n = 6 per group). Liver fibrosis was induced by weekly subcutaneous injection of carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) for eight weeks. Oral gavage of quercetin (50 mg/kg/day) was performed in QR group. Histopathological changes were assessed by hematoxylin-eosin staining, Masson staining and Ishak scoring. Potential targets of quercetin were screened using network pharmacology, followed by protein-protein interaction (PPI) network construction and Gene Ontology (GO)/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses. Cecal microbiota composition was determined by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Parametric or non-parametric tests were used accordingly, including one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test.

Results

Histopathology revealed significant liver injury and fibrosis in the MOD group relative to the CON group. The QR group showed lower Ishak fibrosis scores and milder histopathological features compared with the MOD group. Network pharmacology analysis identified UBC, UBE2I, RBX1, PSMB7 and UBA1 as hub targets, with KEGG pathways of interest including the TNF signaling pathway, p53 signaling pathway, Toll-like receptor signaling pathway and ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis. Alpha diversity of the cecal microbiota differed significantly among groups, whereas beta diversity did not. Relative abundance of Proteobacteria decreased and Firmicutes increased in the QR group relative to the MOD group. Taxa enrichment analysis identified enrichment of Muribaculaceae and Ligilactobacillus in the QR group.

Conclusion

Histopathology and microbiome analyses indicated that quercetin intervention was associated with altered liver histopathological features and shifts in gut microbiota composition in rats with CCl4-induced liver fibrosis. Network pharmacology predicted several hub targets and pathways potentially linked to these observations. As the present analyses are purely correlational and lack mechanistic validation at the molecular level, no causal relationships are implied between the predicted targets/pathways and the observed histological or microbiome changes. These findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and warrant further validation studies.

raw.abstractText:
Background

 Fibrotic liver is one of the serious pathophysiological consequences of chronic injury to the liver, may progress toward serious complications including cirrhosis and hepatic carcinoma.

Objectives

Panax notoginseng is used for both therapeutic and prophylactic purposes in TCM; it is a source of Dencichine, an active substance that has been proven to exhibit antifibrotic properties in hepatic fibrosis. The present study investigated how Dencichine treatment ameliorates liver fibrosis using an animal model and a cellular fibrosis model.

Methods

Randomly assigned, male C57BL/6J mice received 10% CCl4 for 15 consecutive weeks to induce hepatic fibrosis. Treatment with Dencichine was initiated from 7th week onward. To simulate in-vitro the presence of a fibrotic microenvironment, LX-2 cells were treated with PDGF-BB at a concentration of 20 ng/mL and incubated from one up to four days and then treated by various doses of Dencichine. Liver function was evaluated by measuring alanine aminotransferase (ALT), AST, HA and LN. Histopathology was evaluated by haematoxylin/eosin (HE), Masson's trichrome and Sirius red stains. Quantitative real-time PCR and western blot analyses were used to evaluate mRNA and protein expression levels, respectively. Wound-healing assays and transwell chamber experiments were used to assess cell migration; EdU proliferation detection and flow cytometry were performed to measure cell proliferation and cell cycle, respectively.

Results

 The most important results are a considerable reduction of serum concentrations of AST and ALT, HA and laminin in CCl4-treated mice decreased liver injury and ECM deposition. Furthermore, this compound downregulated the expression of cyclin D1 and cyclin E1 and blocked the activation of PI3K and AKT kinases in fibrotic liver cells.

Conclusion

These results indicate that Dencichine may slow the development of liver fibrosis by interfering with the PI3K-AKT signaling cascade, demonstrating significant anti-scarring properties.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Ulcerative colitis is a relapsing inflammatory bowel disease driven by dysregulated immunity, epithelial barrier injury and microbial imbalance. Current therapies remain limited by relapse, adverse effects and incomplete response. Quercetin has anti-inflammatory and barrier-protective activities and ERK-MMP signaling may link inflammation to mucosal tissue damage.

Objectives

To evaluate whether the protective effects of quercetin in experimental ulcerative colitis (UC) are associated with modulation of ERK-MMP signaling, while avoiding causal overinterpretation beyond the animal and cellular evidence.

Methods

A dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model and a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophage inflammatory model were used. Mice were allocated to the control, UC model and low-, medium- and high-dose quercetin groups. Disease activity index (DAI; unitless), colon length, histopathology, inflammatory cytokines and ERK/MMP-related molecules were evaluated by histological staining, ELISA, qRT-PCR and western blotting. In-vitro, quercetin was compared with the ERK phosphorylation inhibitor U0126 and an agonistic stimulus to explore pathway-related associations. The study was exploratory and did not include genetic rescue experiments or human validation.

Results

In DSS-treated mice, medium- and high-dose quercetin were associated with improved colon morphology, reduced DAI scores and partial restoration of colon length. Quercetin decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and increased IL-10 expression. In both mouse colon tissues and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 cells, quercetin was associated with reduced ERK1/2 activation and lower MMP-3 and MMP-9 expression, together with partial recovery of TIMP expression. These molecular changes were directionally consistent with the effects observed after ERK inhibition in-vitro.

Conclusion

Quercetin showed protective effects in experimental UC models and these effects may be associated with modulation of the ERK-MMP signaling axis. Further pathway-specific rescue experiments, pharmacokinetic studies and human-relevant models are required before this mechanism can be considered definitive or clinically translatable.

raw.abstractText: This study aimed to explore the processing mechanism of single medicinal herbs in compound prescriptions, compare the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic changes of Yuanhu Zhitong Formula before and after processing, and elucidate its underlying mechanism against gastric ulcers. The results showed that six components, namely, corydaline, coptisine chloride, palmatine, berberine chloride, phellopterin, and imperatorin, exerted anti-ulcer activities. The optimal vinegar-processing parameters for Corydalis yanhusuo were determined as follows: processing temperature of 84°C, vinegar dosage of 37%, and baking time of 35 min. Vinegar-processed Corydalis yanhusuo could accelerate the in vivo distribution of alkaloid components in the formula, elevate the plasma concentration, and prolong the in vivo retention time of coumarin components. The synergistic effects of the two types of active ingredients endow the vinegar-processed Yuanhu Zhitong Formula with significantly superior antigastric ulcer activity compared with the raw formula. Moreover, network pharmacology results revealed that this formula exerts therapeutic effects against gastric ulcers mainly by regulating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. This study clarified the optimal processing technology and the pharmacodynamic material basis of Yuanhu Zhitong Formula against gastric ulcers, confirmed the efficacy-enhancing effect of processing, and provided data support for the formulation of its processing production standards and clinical medication.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a common vaginal infection in women of reproductive age and is often linked to a vaginal microbiota imbalance. Conventional antibiotics such as metronidazole are effective but are associated with side effects and recurrence, prompting interest in herbal alternatives.

Objectives

To compare the clinical efficacy of medicinal plants versus metronidazole in the treatment of bacterial vaginosis using evidence from randomized clinical trials.

Methods

This narrative review examined randomized clinical trials evaluating herbal interventions for bacterial vaginosis. Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect were searched for studies published up to March 2026. The included studies assessed herbal interventions administered orally or vaginally, alone or with conventional metronidazole therapy. Information on plant species, study design, participants, diagnostic criteria, interventions, results, and conclusions was extracted and synthesized narratively.

Results

Twenty-four published articles were included, covering a range of medicinal plants, including Allium sativum, Myrtus communis, Quercus species, Berberis vulgaris, Zataria multiflora, Calendula officinalis, Cymbopogon olivieri, and others. Herbal therapies showed efficacy comparable to or superior to metronidazole, with fewer side effects and lower recurrence rates. Their effects are attributed to bioactive compounds, including allicin, curcumin, berberine, tannins, flavonoids, and essential oils, which exhibit antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties.

Conclusions

Medicinal plants appear to be safe and effective alternatives or adjuncts for bacterial vaginosis; however, the heterogeneity in study designs and short follow-up periods limits definitive conclusions. Further well-designed, multicenter randomized trials with standardized protocols and long-term follow-up, along with studies exploring individual plants and their mechanisms of action, are needed to confirm efficacy, safety, and reproducibility and to support evidence-based use.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Caffeine is consumed for its presumed cognitive benefits, yet controlled studies have repeatedly failed to find effects on inhibitory control. Cross-sectional work suggests that people with elevated attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms may benefit from chronic, moderate caffeine consumption, but whether acute intake improves cognition in proportion to symptom severity has not been tested experimentally.

Aims

We tested whether 250 mg of caffeine improves active inhibition (withholding a prepared response) and reactive inhibition (resolving response conflict), and whether ADHD symptom severity moderates these effects.

Methods

In a preregistered, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, a nonclinical sample of 36 young adults received 250 mg of caffeine or placebo in counterbalanced order, with testing 45 min after ingestion. Active inhibition was assessed with a Go/No-Go task (204 trials), reactive inhibition with an arrow flanker task (200 trials) and symptoms with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale. Mixed-effects models included treatment, symptom severity, their interaction and ten covariates; Bayes factors quantified evidence for the null.

Results

Both tasks produced their benchmark effects (dz = 1.24 and 1.09) and all indices were reliable (split-half r = 0.73-0.98). Caffeine affected neither commission errors (BF01 = 4.98), response criterion (5.14), Go reaction time (2.83), reaction time variability (4.35), flanker reaction time (5.49) nor flanker accuracy (5.09). ADHD symptoms moderated no effect (15 preregistered tests; smallest p = 0.514), yet predicted performance itself (flanker accuracy r = -0.42), indicating that the null is not due to an insensitive measure.

Conclusions

Caffeine produced no acute benefit for either form of inhibition, and ADHD symptoms did not moderate its effects. Bayes factors supported the absence rather than the nondetection of these effects, arguing against an acute improvement of inhibitory control that scales with ADHD symptom severity in nonclinical young adults. Whether this also holds for chronic consumption or for adults with diagnosed ADHD remains to be tested.

raw.abstractText:
Objective

Caffeine could improve cognitive functions, but study protocols usually prohibit drinking coffee before cognitive testing. However, regular coffee consumers may experience withdrawal effects when they cannot drink their habitual coffee, which may impair cognitive performance. Therefore, we tested the effects of overnight coffee abstinence in regular coffee consumers: once allowing to drink their coffee and once not drinking coffee. The cognitive performance was compared with non-regular coffee consumers.

Methods

Thirty regular coffee consumers (RCCs) and 25 non-regular consumers (N-RCCs) took part in this study. RCCs were tested after their habitual morning coffee (c-RCC) and after overnight abstinence (a-RCC); N-RCCs were tested once. A cognitive battery assessed reaction time (RT), processing speed (digit symbol substitution test), working memory, verbal learning/memory and executive function (Stroop). Sleep quality was included as a covariate.

Results

Compared to c-RCC, overnight coffee abstinence significantly slowed RTs but did not affect the performance in the other cognitive tasks. In the a-RCC condition, but not the c-RCC condition, the RTs were slower than those of the N-RCCs, while accuracy measures were comparable across groups. Sleep quality did not alter these findings.

Conclusions

Overnight coffee abstinence selectively slowed RT, and no statistical support was found for effects on memory or executive function. This suggests that overnight coffee abstinence protocols may introduce withdrawal-related RT slowing as a confound in habitual consumers, whereas other cognitive domains may not be affected. Allowing habitual consumers to maintain normal coffee intake could reduce this bias, supporting tailored rather than uniform abstinence requirements based on the specific outcomes studied.

raw.abstractText: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. raw.abstractText: The collagen triple helix is the most abundant protein structural motif in animals. It tolerates any amino acid in its Xaa and Yaa positions but demands glycine (Gly) at every third position, where the residue packs into the sterically forbidding core of the triple helix and donates the recurring interstrand N-H⋯OC hydrogen bond that stitches the three strands together. (2S)-Proline (Pro) and (2S,4R)-4-hydroxyproline (Hyp) are enriched far above their proteome-wide abundance because they preorganize individual strands into the polyproline II conformation, lowering the entropic cost of folding. We asked whether the triple helix is intrinsically stable enough to form from strands that carry no such preorganization, that is, from polyglycine. To offset the conformational entropy of a Gly-rich tract, we embedded Gly<sub>6</sub> within flanking triple-helical (Pro-Hyp-Gly)<sub>n</sub> clamps in Ac-(Pro-Hyp-Gly)<sub>6</sub>-Gly<sub>6</sub>-(Pro-Hyp-Gly)<sub>5</sub>-Pro-Hyp-NH<sub>2</sub> and compared it with an otherwise identical peptide in which Gly<sub>6</sub> was replaced by two [2-(2-aminoethoxy)ethoxy]acetic acid units, a flexible, length-matched spacer that lacks most of the regularly spaced backbone amides of Gly<sub>6</sub>. Circular dichroism spectroscopy revealed the diagnostic positive band at 225 nm. The molar ellipticity of the spacer-containing control was 86% of that of the Gly<sub>6</sub>-containing peptide, matching the 35/41 = 85% ratio of residues capable of triple-helix formation and consistent with the Gly<sub>6</sub> segment contributing to the triple-helical signal. Thermal denaturation yielded a T<sub>m</sub> of 46.8°C for the Gly<sub>6</sub>-containing peptide, 6.3°C higher than that of the matched spacer control. This added stability indicates that the polyglycine tract is not merely accommodated within the helix but contributes stabilizing interstrand hydrogen bonds. Together, these data indicate that three polyglycine strands can form a collagen triple helix when flanked by triple-helical clamps. This result is consistent with the idea that the triple-helical architecture predates the recruitment of Pro and Hyp, informs the evolutionary origin of collagen, and offers a blunt-ended, symmetric scaffold for designing peptidic triple helices.

While insulin activates the sympathetic nervous system in experimental settings, whether therapeutic insulin administration is associated with cardiac sympathetic predominance under free-living conditions remains unclear. This prospective observational study investigated the association between insulin dosing and cardiac autonomic balance in adults with type 1 diabetes managed exclusively with insulin therapy. Participants underwent continuous heart rate variability (HRV) and glucose monitoring over 4 consecutive days during routine daily activities. Cardiac sympathetic predominance was assessed using the low-frequency power to high-frequency power (LF/HF) ratio derived from HRV analysis, and associations were evaluated using generalized estimating equations. A higher last bolus insulin dose was associated with an increased LF/HF ratio during the early sleep phase. A higher basal insulin dose was also associated with an increased LF/HF ratio during the late sleep phase. These associations persisted after adjustment for mean glucose and mean absolute glucose change during the corresponding sleep phases. Under free-living conditions, higher insulin doses were associated with dose-dependent increases in cardiac sympathetic predominance, independent of glycemic profiles. These findings suggest that insulin dosing may be linked to cardiac autonomic regulation in individuals with type 1 diabetes, highlighting the importance of considering cardiac autonomic balance and potential cardiovascular risk when optimizing insulin therapy.

Article highlights

The relationship between therapeutic insulin administration and cardiac autonomic balance under free-living conditions remains unclear. We examined whether insulin dosing was associated with cardiac sympathetic predominance during daily life in adults with type 1 diabetes managed with insulin therapy. Higher last bolus and basal insulin doses were associated with increased cardiac sympathetic predominance during the early and late sleep phases, respectively, independent of glycemic profiles. These findings suggest that insulin dosing patterns may be linked to cardiac autonomic balance, with potential implications for optimizing insulin therapy in type 1 diabetes.

Background

Prolonged exposure to hepatotoxic antiretroviral therapy (ART) could lead to chronic liver injury, which might increase risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We used causal inference methods to evaluate if cumulative exposure to ART with known mechanisms of chronic liver injury is associated with HCC among people with HIV (PWH), by chronic liver disease (CLD) status.

Methods

We conducted a cohort study of antiretroviral-naive PWH with and without diagnosed CLD who initiated ART in the Veterans Affairs between 1999 and 2023. Exposure to ART with known mechanism of chronic liver injury (mitochondrial toxicity or accumulation of toxic intermediates) was determined monthly through prescription fills. Incident HCC was identified by Veterans Affairs National Cancer Registry and/or recorded diagnoses. Marginal structural models estimated odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of HCC associated with cumulative exposure to chronic liver injury-inducing ART compared with ART without chronic liver injury mechanisms, by CLD status.

Results

Among 11,854 PWH without CLD and 6771 PWH with CLD, we observed 112 and 378 HCC events, respectively. Among PWH without CLD, ≥4 years of exposure to chronic liver injury-inducing ART was associated with HCC when compared with ≥4 years of use of ART without chronic liver injury mechanisms (OR = 4.02 [95% CI: 1.00-16.24]). Among PWH with CLD, ≥4 years of exposure to chronic liver injury-inducing ART was not associated with HCC (OR = 1.36; 95% CI: 0.68-2.72).

Conclusion

Four or more years of ART with a chronic liver injury mechanism was associated with HCC among PWH without CLD, but not those with CLD.

Purpose

To investigate the microbial species latent in corneas of healthy individuals and determine whether small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) serves as a risk factor for pathogen reactivation.

Setting

Ophthalmology Department of Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China.

Design

Prospective cohort study.

Methods

Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) was used to analyze the microbial composition of corneal lenticules from SMILE. Based on the results, patients were categorized into viral group (VG) and nonviral pathogen group (NVPG). 2 Matched groups (MG1 and MG2) were established by selecting pathogen-negative individuals at a 1:4 ratio relative to 2 positive groups. Using SPSS to analyze baseline characteristics, preoperative ocular parameters, and postoperative ocular parameters among groups.

Results

Among the detected pathogens, latent Herpesviruses were identified in 9 cases (4.31%), Papillomavirus were 4 cases (1.91%), and nonviral pathogens were 20 cases (9.57%). Both VG and NVPG groups showed no significant differences in baseline characteristics or preoperative ocular parameters compared with MG groups. In postoperative ocular parameters, no significant differences were found between VG and MG1, although intergroup variations in intraocular pressure and corneal thickness were observed ( P > .05). However, NVPG demonstrated significantly poorer results than MG2 in 1-month spherical equivalent ( P = .033) and corneal epithelial staining ( P = .044).

Conclusions

These findings indicate pathogen latency does not affect ocular status and SMILE surgery is unlikely to reactivate latent viruses or exerts minimal influence. Viral latency has almost no impact on postoperative recovery, while latent nonviral pathogens may interfere with postoperative recovery.

raw.abstractText: Melatonin (MEL) is an endogenous hormone that regulates circadian rhythm, immune function and oxidative stress responses. Norepinephrine (NE), an endogenous catecholamine, increases blood pressure through the sympathetic nervous system and is commonly administered intraoperatively or in the clinically ill patient for hemodynamic support. Although endogenous NE is known to stimulate MEL synthesis, the effects of exogenous intravenous NE on plasma MEL concentration, particularly under general anaesthesia (GA), remain poorly characterised. This study examined the influence of intravenous NE on plasma MEL concentrations in healthy volunteers, both awake and under general anaesthesia. A secondary analysis was conducted using data from a prospective, single-centre, cross-over study involving volunteers who received stepwise NE infusions while awake and under total intravenous general anaesthesia. Arterial blood samples were collected to determine plasma MEL and NE concentrations. Linear mixed-effects modelling was used to assess the relationship between NE and MEL concentrations. A total of 36 healthy volunteers were enroled, yielding 417 MEL-NE samples. Intravenous NE administration was significantly associated with higher plasma MEL concentration, corresponding to an estimated 26% increase in MEL per 1 standard-deviation increase in NE concentration (Estimate = 0.230, p < 0.001). MEL concentrations were approximately 43% higher in the awake phase compared to GA (Estimate = 0.356, p < 0.001). GA did not significantly modify the NE-MEL association (Estimate = -0.02877, p = 0.528). Substantial positive correlation was observed between baseline MEL concentrations and the magnitude of the response to NE administration (r = 0.74). In conclusion, intravenous NE increases plasma MEL concentrations in both awake and anaesthetised individuals. Substantial interindividual variation in MEL response suggests underlying physiological differences. Future studies should explore the long-term effects of NE administration on MEL concentrations. Background

Sleep deprivation and poor sleep quality are critical problems among intensive care unit (ICU) patients, with significant implications for recovery, delirium onset and clinical outcomes. Despite growing scientific interest, no bibliometric study has systematically mapped the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of this field.

Aim

To analyse the bibliometric characteristics and thematic structure of publications on sleep deprivation, sleep promotion and sleep quality in ICU patients indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 1983 and 2026.

Study design

A descriptive and evaluative bibliometric analysis was conducted. Data were retrieved on April 26, 2026, from the WoS Core Collection using a comprehensive search strategy. Publications were filtered by document type, WoS categories (nursing, critical care medicine, anaesthesiology) and index (SCI-EXPANDED, SSCI, ESCI). Data were analysed using R software with the Biblioshiny interface, and annual publication trends were evaluated using Microsoft Excel.

Results

Of 11 418 publications retrieved, 379 met the inclusion criteria, spanning 37 years (1983-2026). Linear regression revealed a statistically significant positive trend in publication output (β = 0.643, R2 = 0.704, r = 0.839, p < 0.001), with mean annual publications of 10.24 ± 8.83 and notable acceleration from the 2000s onwards. Thematic mapping identified 'sleep', 'sleep deprivation' and 'delirium' as motor themes both highly central and well developed. Emerging concepts included circadian rhythm, actigraphy, fatigue, pain and anxiety.

Conclusions

ICU sleep research has grown substantially over four decades, with sleep deprivation and delirium emerging as co-dominant research priorities. Thematic gaps and emerging clusters identified in this analysis highlight important directions for future nursing research and evidence-based practice development in critical care.

Relevance to clinical practice

This bibliometric analysis identified sleep deprivation and delirium as the co-dominant motor themes of ICU sleep research, and intervention-related concepts such as earplugs, eye masks and melatonin as emerging clusters. These evidence-based trends can guide ICU nurses in prioritizing targeted sleep promotion protocols and support policymakers in directing resources toward the most scientifically mature intervention areas in critical care.

raw.abstractText: Preterm white matter injury (PWMI) is a serious neurologic condition that threatens neonatal survival and severely impairs the cognitive and motor development of affected children. Melatonin (Mel), a neuroendocrine hormone with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, has shown neuroprotective potential in neonatal brain injury, although the mechanisms underlying its effects in PWMI remain incompletely understood. Multimodal MRI can provide a useful noninvasive approach for monitoring treatment-related changes in white matter injury and development, supporting further investigation of Mel as a potential therapeutic strategy for PWMI.

raw.abstractText: TYRO3, AXL, and MERTK, the TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), play roles in phagocytosis and negative regulation of immune responses, contributing to homeostasis in many adult tissues. Aberrant TAM signaling leads to diseases including autoimmune disorders, viral infection, inflammation, and cancer. Development of successful drugs targeting TAM receptors is hindered by incomplete knowledge of the receptor activation mechanism. Receptor dimerization is assumed to play a role, as seen for most RTKs. However, full biological responses require the TAM ligands to engage phosphatidylserine in an opposing cell or virus membrane, suggesting a more complex mechanism, possibly involving higher-order receptor oligomerization or clustering. Here, we present an X-ray crystal structure of the ectodomain of MERTK, which adopts a highly curved conformation with key interdomain boundaries stabilized by N-linked glycan moieties. We show that this MERTK extracellular region (ECR) forms a similar conformation in solution using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), which also suggests a flexible ECR. We compare these crystallographic and solution data for MERTK with SAXS and AlphaFold structural predictions for the other two TAM receptors. SAXS data confirm that each TAM ECR has a distinct curvature, with TYRO3 the most bent and AXL relatively straight. This leads us to speculate that these different ectodomain conformations guide receptor-specific functions. The MERTK X-ray crystal structure also suggests a head-to-tail intermolecular interaction between the Ig2 domain of one MERTK and the FNIIIb domain of a second that has intriguing parallels with interactions that have been proposed to regulate Eph receptor clustering.

raw.abstractText: Activity-guided separation of medicinal plants requires linking activity signals and chromatographic resolution in complex matrices. In this study, based on a previously established HPLC-DPPH platform, medium-pressure prefractionation and preparative chromatographic purification were applied for the targeted isolation of free radical scavengers from Saxifraga tangutica (S. tangutica). Medium-pressure prefractionation reduced sample complexity and enriched active fractions, while Click XION chromatography concentrated the target fraction. Subsequent purification on the ReproSil-Pur C18 AQ column resolved this fraction into two baseline-separated active peaks, affording compounds with purities greater than 95%. The isolated compounds were identified as quercetin-3-O-β-D-glucoside-7-O-β-D-glucoside and quercetin-3-O-β-D-galactoside-7-O-β-D-glucoside, a pair of C-4″-epimeric quercetin 3,7-di-O-glycosides. Both compounds exhibited DPPH radical-scavenging activity, with IC<sub>50</sub> values of 68.94 ± 2.77 and 75.59 ± 2.14 μM, respectively. DFT calculations, molecular docking, and ADMET prediction further supported the comparative interpretation of their electronic features, antioxidant-related interaction potential, and predicted pharmacokinetic profiles. Overall, this study achieved the activity guided isolation and activity evaluation of a pair of high-purity C-4″-epimeric flavonol diglycosides from S. tangutica, providing a practical chromatographic strategy for the targeted characterization of structurally similar bioactive constituents from medicinal plants.

raw.abstractText: Ripened washed-rind and long-ripened cheeses owe their prized sulfurous, savory character to intensive proteolysis and amino-acid catabolism; the same activity, when poorly controlled, also generates sensory off-flavors and toxic biogenic amines (BAs). Histamine and tyramine reach up to approximately 2000-2500 and 1000-2000 mg/kg in extreme samples, although most cheeses contain far less, so that a 30-g portion of a high-histamine cheese can exceed the 50-mg per-meal intake regarded as without adverse effect in healthy adults. Flavor formation and chemical safety have traditionally been studied apart. This critical review reframes them as two outcomes of one metabolism: Proteolysis liberates a shared free amino-acid pool from which volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs) and BAs arise. Because the principal VSCs derive from methionine whereas the major BAs derive from histidine, tyrosine, ornithine, arginine, and lysine, we treat the branches not as direct competitors for one substrate but as metabolically coupled fates linked by shared proteolytic supply, overlapping physicochemical controls and microbial cross-feeding. Integrating evidence across cheese families, we reclassify the ripening microbiota into condition-dependent functional guilds, formalize metabolic bivalence (organisms that both generate flavor and degrade amines), and define a sensory inflection point separating the windowed VSC dose-response from the monotonic BA hazard. We critically appraise multi-omics, volatilomics, biosensors, machine learning, and digital twins, and outline a precision-fermentation roadmap. Current, largely in vitro, and single-variety evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, controllable decoupling, which we frame as a testable hypothesis that recasts cheese quality as a controllable metabolic-allocation problem.

raw.abstractText: Prosthetic heart valve development consists of several branching, innovative strategies to mediate the complex native environment that wears down valve durability. Anti-calcification treatments are being applied to pericardial tissue, durable polymers are being developed that mitigate oxidative degradation and stress cracking, and heart valve tissue engineering has introduced resorbable scaffolds that can develop into stable, functional tissue. In each case, an increasing breadth of strategies is being developed to curb the persistent issue of valve deterioration. This study aimed to synthesize and characterize an ascorbic acid-containing polyurethane to impart antioxidant properties to degradable scaffolds for tissue engineered heart valve (TEHV) replacement. Blends of poly(carbonate-ascorbic acid) urethane (PCAU) and poly(carbonate urethane) urea (PCUU) were fabricated into microporous scaffolds to evaluate the impact of PCAU in vitro on mechanics, degradation, cell viability, calcification, bacterial adhesion, and in vivo on native tissue response in a juvenile rat subcutaneous model. PCAU blended with PCUU in a 25:75 ratio (PCAU-25) had mechanical properties similar to PCUU, while higher concentrations of PCAU were not mechanically robust. PCAU-25 showed greater reactive oxygen species (ROS) inhibition and degradation, and reduced calcification and bacterial adhesion in vitro. In a juvenile rat subcutaneous model, both PCUU and PCAU-25 groups showed negligible calcification after 4 weeks. PCAU-25, however, showed much greater cell infiltration and immune response, possibly due to an accelerated rate of degradation. PCAU-25 was then fabricated into a polymeric valve scaffold and underwent basic mechanical and hydrodynamic performance assessment that demonstrated function similar to PCUU valves previously reported. These findings demonstrate proof-of-concept for a new polyurethane formulation incorporating ascorbic acid for antioxidant bioactivity and translatability into a functional TEHV scaffold.

raw.abstractText: Vitamin D is a nutrient and prohormone obtained from diet and supplements and synthesized in the skin. It is essential for calcium and phosphate homeostasis and skeletal health and influences multiple extra-skeletal processes, yet deficiency remains common worldwide. This narrative review summarizes vitamin D sources, physiology, metabolism, pharmacokinetics, clinical relevance and safety and outlines the distinct pharmacokinetic profiles and clinical roles of vitamin D, calcidiol and calcitriol and its analogues. Evidence consistently supports vitamin D, combined with calcium, for preventing and treating deficiency-related skeletal disorders in high-risk populations, and in specific conditions such as malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, hypoparathyroidism and frailty. In vitamin D-replete populations, large trials show limited extra-skeletal benefits, apart from modest effects on cancer mortality and progression from prediabetes to Type 2 diabetes. Untargeted screening is not recommended. Future research should prioritize targeted supplementation, standardized assays and identification of populations most likely to benefit from supplementation.

raw.abstractText:
Purpose of review

Pharmacotherapy is widely used to manage neuropsychiatric sequelae that may interfere with neurorehabilitation after traumatic brain injury (TBI), despite limited TBI-specific evidence. This review summarizes psychopharmacological evidence from the past 18 months and proposes a three-step approach: deprescribing potentially recovery-limiting medications, characterizing individual neuropsychiatric symptoms, and selecting symptom-targeted treatments to support cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and functional recovery after TBI.

Recent findings

Methylphenidate shows the most consistent evidence for selected cognitive outcomes, particularly attention and processing speed. Pharmacological approaches to agitation, sleep-wake disorders, depression, fatigue, and posttraumatic headache have been studied, but TBI-specific evidence remains limited or heterogeneous. Sedative, anticholinergic, and cognitive adverse effects, cardiovascular risks, and dependence require consideration in TBI neurorehabilitation.

Summary

No pharmacological treatment is established as disease-modifying after TBI. Given the limited evidence, psychopharmacotherapy should be individualized, symptom-targeted, and integrated into multidisciplinary TBI neurorehabilitation. Continuous medication review and deprescribing should accompany careful treatment selection and monitoring. Future trials should determine whether symptom improvement translates into better rehabilitation participation, functional independence, and long-term health-related quality of life.

raw.abstractText: Marked differences in solubility and stability between hydrophilic bioactive peptides and hydrophobic carotenoids constrain their synergistic oral delivery. Building on the complementary activities of Meretrix meretrix-derived immunomodulatory peptide (MMIP) and astaxanthin (AST), this study developed co-loaded nanoparticles, HLC10, featuring a BSA-dextran glycoprotein core and a composite outer layer of hyaluronic acid (HA) and yeast β-glucan. Hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic forces collectively drive the multicomponent assembly. By tuning particle interfacial hydration and the dispersion state of the payloads, the formulation improved co-encapsulation capacity, processing and storage stability, and gastrointestinal bioaccessibility of MMIP and AST. The composite polysaccharide outer layer further increased particle accumulation in Peyer's patches-associated regions and increased uptake by RAW264.7 macrophages. Oral HLC10 administration ameliorated cyclophosphamide-induced immunosuppression, restored immune organ and ileal architecture, and produced coordinated shifts in gut microbiota, fecal short-chain fatty acids, and spleen nucleotide-related metabolic profiles. These findings support the immunomodulatory potential of HLC10, but the evidence remains largely limited to endpoint measures in animal models, and direct validation of cellular functions and the underlying mechanisms is still required. Overall, this stratified co-assembly strategy offers a feasible route for the synergistic oral delivery of food-derived active ingredients with markedly different physicochemical properties.

raw.abstractText: Antimicrobial resistance is a global public health concern, and appropriate antimicrobial use in food-producing animal medicine requires accurate bacteriological diagnosis. However, the effectiveness of bacteriological training and the reliability of in-house antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) in food-animal practice remain unclear. We assessed preliminary organism identification accuracy and the impact of a bacteriological training program among bovine veterinarians affiliated with NOSAI Hokkaido, Japan, and evaluated disk diffusion AST variability using the same Escherichia coli isolate. Preliminary identification accuracy increased from 37% (35/94) before training to 91% (86/94) immediately afterward. Pre-training accuracy was significantly higher among frequent testers than among participants who performed no routine bacteriological testing, whereas post-training accuracy was high across all three testing-frequency groups. In the AST assessment, inhibition zone diameters varied substantially across all six antimicrobial disks, and discordant susceptible/resistant (S/R) interpretations occurred in more than 50% of participants for two agents. Multivariable generalized estimating equation analyses showed that smear technique was significantly associated with discordant S/R interpretations, whereas agar medium was not significantly associated with discordance after adjustment. The association between inoculum quantity and discordance could not be reliably established because only two participants were classified in the appropriate-inoculum category. These findings demonstrate the immediate benefit of structured practical training for improving preliminary organism identification and highlight the need to standardize field-based AST, particularly smear technique. Wider adoption of the simplified disk diffusion procedures described in the national mastitis guidebook may improve AST consistency in clinical practice.

raw.abstractText: Rapid bacterial identification could help guide antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), but image-based classification must generalise across bacterial strains. We developed SC-MAPS, a multichannel microscopy dataset comprising 916,435 single cells from 13 bacterial species, with independent strains reserved for evaluation. Combining phase-contrast and fluorescence information using deep learning achieved 65.4% single-cell species-classification accuracy on held-out strains. To assess whether imperfect species predictions retained useful information for downstream testing, we defined eight antimicrobial-resistance-informed AST-routing groups. Pooling species probabilities increased routing accuracy to 77.1%, rising to 91.1% when predictions from five cells were combined and 96.2% with 20 cells. Synthetic mixtures revealed limitations in minority-species recovery, while exploratory analysis of unseen organisms demonstrated the potential for out-of-distribution detection. SC-MAPS provides a framework for investigating transferable bacterial phenotypes and developing image-based identification and AST-routing strategies.

raw.abstractText: Cellular immunotherapies have transformed oncologic treatment in recent years, yet the inability to monitor cell migration post-transfusion remains a significant barrier to their development. Here, we explore the feasibility of a non-invasive cell-tracking method utilizing Cu(I)-catalyzed click chemistry in which cells are first labeled with alkynes and, after 1-2 weeks, are selectively targeted via an azide-conjugated fluorescent probe. We developed Click1, a novel tris-Cu-chelating azide capable of a rapid, robust click reaction directly on live cell surfaces with minimal cytotoxicity. When paired with Click1, two distinct alkyne-labeling reagents, N-(4-pentynoyl)-mannosamine-tetraacylated (Ac4ManNAl) and propargyl choline, were capable of detecting human T cells for over two weeks. Our findings elucidate the metabolic turnover of biochemical handles in primary immune cells, providing a potential framework for long-term cell tracking in immunotherapies.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Periodontitis is a widespread chronic inflammatory condition that frequently coexists with diabetes mellitus (DM). Identifying non-invasive biomarkers is essential for early detection, targeted therapy, and better understanding of the bidirectional relationship between these two diseases. This study aimed to investigate salivary metabolomic profiles in diabetic individuals with and without periodontitis to identify candidate metabolites associated with periodontitis in patients with diabetes.

Methods

This pilot study compared salivary 1H NMR metabolomic profiles of patients with diabetes with and without periodontitis (n = 13 per group). Unstimulated whole saliva was collected from both groups. Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) was applied to differentiate between the groups. Spectral variables with VIP > 1 were selected for metabolite annotation, followed by metabolite set enrichment analysis (MSEA) to identify dysregulated metabolic pathways.

Results

Using the PLS-DA model, a total of 78 discriminating variables were identified, leading to the annotation of ten key metabolites: glycolic acid, thymidine, tyramine, deoxyguanosine, cytidine, uridine, NADPH, ADP, serotonin, and nicotinate. MSEA revealed significant pathway disturbances, with pyrimidine metabolism emerging as a notably enriched pathway.

Conclusion

The metabolomics study of saliva using 1H NMR showed distinct metabolic disturbances, particularly in pyrimidine metabolism, in diabetic periodontitis. Although these altered metabolites could serve as potential candidates for non-invasive biomarkers, independent validation from a large cohort is still required before they can be translated into clinical diagnostic use.

raw.authorString: Shrestha D, Bajracharya B, Shah P, Shrestha P, Ghimire S, Paudel SR, Dangol S, Shrestha P, Rajbanshi S, Ranjitkar P, Chand S, Sharma M, Sardar CK, Tuladhar R, Bajracharya S, Karna AK, Manandhar KD, Mahato RK, Dahal G, Williams T, Kelly-Hope LA.
raw.abstractText:
Background:

In Nepal, lymphatic filariasis (LF), caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, remains a priority neglected tropical disease targeted for elimination by 2030. Despite large-scale mass drug administration (MDA) and post-MDA surveillance, focal transmission may persist. Molecular xenomonitoring (MX) of mosquito vectors is a complementary method for detecting ongoing transmission. This study assessed mosquito abundance and species composition and compared gravid traps and CDC light traps for capturing Culex quinquefasciatus, the primary LF vector. It examined spatial and seasonal vector patterns, W. bancrofti infection rates, and climatic associations across three LF endemic districts. Methodology: A longitudinal entomological survey was conducted from September 2022 to September 2023 in selected sites of Dhading, Jhapa, and Kapilvastu districts using gravid traps and CDC light traps. Mosquitoes were morphologically identified to species level, and female Cx. quinquefasciatus were pooled (up to 25 mosquitoes) for detection of W. bancrofti DNA using real-time PCR. Mosquito abundance, species composition, trap efficiency, spatial variation (within and between locations), temporal trends (daily, weekly, monthly, seasonal), infection rate (pool positivity, and maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) of infection using PoolTestR package in R software), and climatic associations (precipitation, temperature, humidity) were analysed.

Results:

A total of 60,922 mosquitoes belonging to eight genera (Culex, Anopheles, Aedes, Armigeres, Malaya, Mansonia, Tripteroides, and Toxorhynchites) were identified. Of these, 16,044 were female Cx. quinquefasciatus. Gravid traps showed higher relative trapping efficiency of female Cx. quinquefasciatus than light traps, with the highest efficiency observed in Jhapa (3.60:1). Temporal trends varied across locations; however, overall Cx. quinquefasciatus abundance peaked during the spring and summer months (March-May), coinciding with the monsoon period, and was positively correlated with climatic factors. W. bancrofti infection rates varied by location and trap type, with gravid traps yielding higher infection rates, particularly in Jhapa. A total of 785 pools of Cx. quinquefasciatus were screened. Pool positivity and infection prevalence (MLE) ranged from 10.3% to 17.6% and 0.5% to 0.9% in Dhading, 12.5% to 36.8% and 0.9% to 2.0% in Jhapa, and 5.3% to 20.0% and 0.3% to 1.5% in Kapilvastu, respectively.

Conclusions:

The study highlights ongoing transmission in three LF-endemic areas of Nepal, emphasising the need for continued surveillance in high-risk areas and periods. Gravid trap-based xenomonitoring could complement community-based W. bancrofti surveillance by identifying hotspots and optimising the timing and targeting of LF elimination interventions.

raw.abstractText:
Background

Saroglitazar, a dual PPAR alpha/gamma agonist, improved serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels in patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) in a phase 2a clinical trial.

Methods

EPICS-III is a phase 2b/3 adaptive, double-blind, randomized controlled trial in patients with PBC who had an inadequate response to or were intolerant of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). In phase 2b, 37 participants received placebo or saroglitazar magnesium 1 or 2 mg for 16 weeks. Saroglitazar magnesium 1 mg (0.97 mg of saroglitazar) was selected for phase 3, which randomized 148 patients to saroglitazar (n=97) or placebo (n=51) for 52 weeks. The primary endpoint was biochemical response at week 52, defined as ALP <1.67 x ULN with ≥15% reduction from baseline and total bilirubin below ULN; the key secondary endpoint was ALP normalization.

Results

Baseline characteristics in the phase 3 efficacy population were comparable except for higher baseline ALP and other liver biochemistries in the saroglitazar group. Biochemical response was achieved in 56.7% versus 9.8% with placebo (difference, 48.0%; 95% CI, 35.3 to 60.8; p<0.001). Among participants with baseline ALP ≤3xULN, biochemical response rates were 79.0% versus 14.3%, and 83.1% versus 14.7% in the per-protocol analysis. ALP normalization occurred in 8.2% with saroglitazar versus 0% with placebo (difference, 8.5%; 95% CI, 2.9 to 14; p=0.016). Among participants with baseline 5-D Itch score ≥12, the week-24 treatment difference was -3.2 points (95% CI, -5.66 to -0.82) but was not maintained at week 52. Adverse events occurred in 81.1% with saroglitazar versus 90.5% with placebo, and serious adverse events occurred in 6.3% and 11.1%, respectively.

Conclusion

Saroglitazar 0.97 mg significantly improved biochemical response and ALP normalization and was well tolerated over 52 weeks.

raw.abstractText: To address the challenge of the trade-off between mechanical properties and thermal conductivity in magnesium alloys, Mg-xSn-0.2Ca-0.5Zr alloys (x = 3, 4, 5 wt.%) were investigated in this work. Permanent mold casting, semi-solid rheo-die casting, and heat treatment were employed to tailor the microstructure of the alloys. The inherent correlations between microstructure evolution, mechanical properties, and thermal conductivity were systematically explored. The results reveal that as Sn content increases in permanent mold cast alloys, grain refinement occurs and the volume fraction of secondary phases rises. Nevertheless, excessive Sn induces coarsening of grain-boundary Mg 2 Sn, thereby degrading both ductility and thermal conductivity. Among the permanent mold cast alloys, Mg-4Sn-0.2Ca-0.5Zr exhibits optimal overall performance, with an ultimate tensile strength of 137 MPa, yield strength of 71 MPa, elongation of 7.6%, and thermal conductivity of 86.12 W/(m·K), and is accompanied by the lowest hot-tearing susceptibility. Near-spherical α-Mg grains are obtained in the semi-solid rheo-die cast Mg-4Sn-0.2Ca-0.5Zr alloy. After T6 heat treatment, fine Mg 2 Sn precipitates are dispersed throughout the matrix. The ultimate tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation are improved to 202 MPa, 112 MPa, and 11.7%, respectively. Meanwhile, aging facilitates the precipitation of Sn from the α-Mg matrix and reduces electron scattering, contributing to an elevated thermal conductivity of 110.68 W/(m·K). Regulation of the solidification microstructure enables the simultaneous enhancement of strength, ductility, and thermal conductivity for Mg-Sn-Ca-Zr alloys.

raw.authorString: Hawezy HJS, Ali LIA.
raw.abstractText: Water contamination is a crucial ecological concern impacting aquatic ecosystems and human health, particularly because of heavy metals entering water bodies from the industrial, agricultural, and mining activities. To address this, magnesium-doped cobalt ferrite nanoparticles (MgCoFe 2 O 4 @SiO 2 -CPTMS-Cur) were expanded for effective heavy metal removal from wastewater. These nanoparticles were made initially through coprecipitation technique and then were coated with silica and modified with 3-chloropropyltrimethoxysilane (CPTMS) and curcumin (Cur) to improve the adsorption capabilities. The as-synthesized product was fully characterised by FTIR, EDX, XRD, TEM SEM, BET, TGA and VSM, showing a crystalline structure and a porous surface with a BET surface area of 24.176 m 2 /g. The adsorption experiments showed an effective removal of Lead Pb(II) and Cadmium Cd(II), with a maximum abilities of 259.50 mg/g for Pb(II) and 208.35 mg/g for Cd(II). Kinetic testing revealed that the adsorption followed a second-order kinetic model, despite the Langmuir isotherm model accurately representing the equilibrium data. The adsorption process was endothermic, spontaneous, and beneficial, according to thermodynamic study. Research on regeneration demonstrated the durability and reusability of the composite over four cycles, highlighting its promise as a frugal and operative adsorbent for heavy metal extraction in environmental cleanup. The effective removal of Pb(II) and Cd(II) metal ions from tap, groundwater, and lake water was achieved utilising this innovative adsorbent.

raw.abstractText: Crown gall disease, caused by Agrobacterium vitis, is a global threat to viticulture that severely compromises vine vigor and berry quality. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying grapevine resistance, five cultivars were inoculated with A. vitis strain A10 under controlled greenhouse conditions. Pathological assessments revealed divergent disease progression patterns among cultivars in which Yan73 (Y73) and Muscat Blanc (MB) exhibited higher resistance, whereas Y73 displayed mild disease development. Conversely, Merlot (ML), Cabernet Sauvignon, and Chardonnay showed rapid symptom development, and ML was identified as the most susceptible, characterized by the highest incidence and severity. Given that bacterial pathogens such as A. vitis are notoriously difficult to eradicate after infection, characterizing the early infection phase is critical for effective management. Comparative transcriptional analysis (RNA-seq) was conducted to capture the early molecular responses across these cultivars. Differentially expressed genes shared among cultivars were significantly enriched in pathways related to plant-pathogen interaction, stilbene biosynthesis, and responses to oxygen levels. Notably, ethylene signaling and response pathways were predominantly enriched in the relatively resistant cultivars Y73 and MB, suggesting their pivotal role in early defense. Further investigation into the stilbene synthase (STS) pathway revealed that its primary catalytic product, resveratrol (Res), serves as a key defensive metabolite. In vivo assays demonstrated that exogenous Res treatments significantly attenuated disease incidence and severity in a dose-dependent manner. Overall, this study outlines the early immune response of grapevine to A. vitis infection and highlights the importance of STS and ethylene pathways in resistance, providing potential targets for breeding crown gall-resistant grape cultivars.

raw.abstractText: Modern dietary patterns are increasingly dominated by highly processed foods rich in advanced glycation end-products (AGEs). Although dietary AGE intake has been epidemiologically linked to pulmonary diseases, its systemic impact on the distal pulmonary microenvironment remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the effects of a chronic high-AGE diet on the pulmonary microbiota and metabolites in female C57BL/6 mice. Results showed that high-AGE intake induced significant pulmonary structural damage, evidenced by a reduced lung-to-body weight ratio. Concurrently, it provoked systemic inflammation, marked by an elevated blood eosinophil percentage and a markedly increased neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio. 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealed pulmonary taxon-specific alterations in the high-AGE group, characterized by enrichment of potentially pathogenic, strictly anaerobic, and proteolytic Gram-negative bacteria in lung tissue, alongside depletion of beneficial immunomodulatory and short-chain fatty acid-producing commensals in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Functional predictions further indicated significant downregulation of amino acid biosynthesis (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan), vitamin B6 metabolism, and ABC transport systems in the high-AGE group. Metabolomics confirmed that pulmonary essential amino acid biosynthesis was affected by high-AGE intake. Collectively, our study provides important evidence that dietary AGEs fundamentally reshape the pulmonary microbial and metabolic ecosystem, underscoring the diet-lung axis as a potential critical target for respiratory health in the context of industrialized modern diets.

raw.abstractText:
Background

While observational studies have explored the association between gout, uric acid (UA) levels, and the risk of epilepsy, their findings remain inconsistent.

Objectives

To clarify the potential causal relationship, we performed a Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis.

Material and methods

We conducted a bidirectional MR analysis using genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary data. Epilepsy data were sourced from the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE), gout data from the FinnGen consortium and a GWAS of clinically defined gout and its subtypes, and UA data from the BioBank Japan (BBJ) and a genome-wide meta-analysis of serum UA levels in Japanese individuals. The inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method served as the primary causal inference approach. To ensure robustness, we complemented this with 3 additional methods: MR-Egger, weighted median, and MR using Robust Adjusted Profile Score (MR-RAPS) - the latter specifically employed to account for potential weak instrument bias due to the limited number of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) included in this analysis.

Results

Our analysis identified a causal association between genetically predicted gout and an increased risk of epilepsy (odds ratio (OR) = 1.014, 95% confidence interval (95% CI): 1.011-1.017, p < 0.001), generalized epilepsy (OR = 1.009, 95% CI: 1.000-1.018, p = 0.042), and focal epilepsy (OR = 1.044, 95% CI: 1.002-1.088, p = 0.041) in Europeans. In contrast, UA levels showed no significant association with epilepsy or its subtypes in this population. Similarly, neither gout nor UA levels were linked to epilepsy in East Asians. Sensitivity analyses generally supported the robustness of the primary findings.

Conclusions

This MR study provides genetic evidence supporting a potential causal role of gout in increasing the risk of epilepsy, including generalized and focal epilepsy, in European populations. In contrast, genetically predicted UA levels showed no significant association with epilepsy. These findings support a potential role of gout in epilepsy risk and warrant further investigation into the underlying mechanisms.

Objectives

Urine cultures are frequently collected in hospitalized children for urinary tract infection (UTI) screening, despite often being unnecessary, invasive, and resource intensive. We aimed to decrease the proportion of unnecessary urine cultures in admitted children aged 90 days to 24 months from 65% to 45% over 1 year.

Methodology

The Model for Improvement guided problem understanding and change ideas. The main intervention included a 2-step UTI screening pathway previously implemented at our institution's emergency department with emphasis on completing point-of-care urinalysis (UA) on noninvasive urine bag sample. If positive for pyuria, bladder catheterization was performed for urine culture. Additional interventions included electronic medical record order set, education, interdisciplinary collaboration, and alignment with the institution's Choosing Wisely program. The primary outcome was the proportion of urine cultures completed without preceding positive UA screen. The balancing measure was the number of missed UTIs. Analysis used Statistical Process Control charts.

Results

Baseline data (April 2020-March 2021) demonstrated that 65% of urine cultures were collected without a preceding positive UA. Postintervention data (April 2021-January 2025) demonstrated a decreased proportion of urine cultures collected without preceding positive UA screen from 65% to 22%. Special cause variation was detected 1 year following implementation of the pathway with sustained change during the study period. There was no increase in missed UTIs.

Conclusions

Process standardization using 2-step UTI screening pathway reduced unnecessary invasive urine culture collection in hospitalized children. The novel spread of this initiative to inpatient pediatric units aligns with best practices promoting high-value care.

Purpose

Evaluating micronutrient deficiencies in the critically ill population is challenging given the complex clinical picture for many patients. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is a risk factor for micronutrient deficiencies in this cohort, with deficiencies resulting from increased losses in dialysis effluent or adsorption to tubing or to the dialysis filter. The aim of this article is to summarize pertinent research literature regarding micronutrient supplementation and monitoring in CRRT and identify areas for pharmacists to improve patient outcomes from a nutrition standpoint.

Summary

A computerized literature search was conducted of the PubMed electronic database, and articles were included if they discussed one of the prespecified micronutrients and renal replacement therapy. The micronutrients specifically addressed in this article are copper, selenium, zinc, L-carnitine, vitamin C, vitamin B1, vitamin B6, and vitamin B9. For each of these micronutrients, we summarize the evidence for deficiencies in CRRT and supplementation strategies. However, in many cases, literature is lacking to support supplementation and monitoring strategies specifically in CRRT.

Conclusion

Current literature recognizes that standard supplementation may not be enough in the critically ill population on CRRT, but evidence is lacking for optimal micronutrient supplementation doses and monitoring parameters. Until future literature is available, pharmacists should be aware of these deficiencies and help guide recommendations for supplementation.

raw.abstractText: The GABA  B receptor is a central regulator of neuronal transmission and excitability by pre- and postsynaptic mechanisms. Its dysfunction causes severe neurological disease, but the underlying pathomechanisms remain elusive. Here, we exploit a distinct CNS autoimmune disorder in which patients develop specific autoantibodies against GABA  B receptors causing autoimmune encephalitis with severe memory dysfunction and epilepsy. We demonstrate that human autoantibodies target the sushi-domains of the GABA  B receptor B1a subunit and the B2 subunit and interfere with presynaptic signaling. This specific presynaptic pathology results from exclusive functional antagonism of the B1a subunit and disrupts short- and long-term synaptic plasticity, abnormally amplifies hippocampal network oscillations and coupling  in vivo , and ultimately impairs memory consolidation. Our results demonstrate that autoimmune presynaptic pathomechanisms alone are sufficient to interfere with memory processing, thus defining a causal link between molecular GABA  B receptor disturbance, synaptic pathology, circuit dysfunction, and dementia distinct from classical neurodegenerative processes.

raw.abstractText: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is an important and significant reason for cancer-related morbidity and mortality globally. Treatment remains challenging due to recurrence, metastasis, and chemoresistance. Evidence shows that oxidative stress, ongoing inflammation, and cancer stem cells (CSCs) play essential functions in CRC development and progression. Nrf2 is a master regulator of cellular redox balance through the Keap1-Nrf2-is signalling pathway. Normal activation of Nrf2 protects colonic cells from oxidative DNA harm and inflammation during initial carcinogenesis. However, sustained Nrf2 activation in tumours encourages chemoresistance, metabolic reprogramming, and CSC upkeep, showing a dual role. Traditional medicine and dietary phytochemicals (curcumin, sulforaphane, resveratrol, EGCG, berberine) can modulate Nrf2 while interacting with NF-κB, Wnt/β-catenin, and Notch pathways. This review synthesises mechanistic and translational evidence on Nrf2 modulation in CRC chemoprevention, stressing conventional medicine-derived agents in modern approaches. It moreover highlights difficulties, limitations, and future viewpoints for precision chemoprevention and personalised interventions.

Introduction

This guideline establishes recommendations for the treatment of SWD.

Methods

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) commissioned a task force of experts in sleep and circadian medicine to develop recommendations and assign strengths based on a systematic review of the literature and an assessment of the evidence using the GRADE process. The task force summarized the relevant literature and the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations supporting the recommendations. The AASM Board of Directors approved the final recommendations.

Recommendations

The following recommendations are intended as a guide for clinicians in choosing specific treatment(s) for symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or insomnia, and for circadian adaptation in adults with SWD. Each recommendation statement is assigned a strength (e.g., "Strong" or "Conditional"). For SWD, there were only "conditional" recommendations for or against (i.e., "We suggest…") and those requiring the clinician to use clinical knowledge and experience and consider the individual patient's values and preferences to determine the best course of action. Interventions in recommendation statements were compared to no treatment. Adults with SWD with symptoms of excessive sleepiness associated with work schedule: 1. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of armodafinil or modafinil taken 30 to 60 minutes prior to the night shift over no armodafinil or modafinil (Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). 2. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Individuals with SWD who exhibit insomnia and daytime function impairments may also benefit from using bright light during their night shift. 3. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of caffeine taken prior to and/or during the night shift over no caffeine (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 4. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of a clockwise rotating shift schedule over a counterclockwise rotating shift schedule (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 5. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests taking a nap over no nap prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Sleep inertia occurring soon after the nap may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleep inertia prior to driving or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 6. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests either not eating or eating a snack rather than eating a full meal during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 7. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of caffeine and bright light over the combination of no caffeine and no bright light (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 8. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of taking a nap and caffeine over the combination of no nap and no caffeine prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia: 9. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia the AASM suggests the use of CBT-I over no CBT-I (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 10. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia following the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 11. In adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia, when transitioning from daytime to nighttime sleep, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin for night sleep following shift work (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 12. In adults with SWD who desire to take a nap prior to the first night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin prior to the nap (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

Melatonin may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleepiness prior to driving, returning to work or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 13. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of ramelteon or other melatonin receptor agonists over no melatonin receptor agonist (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 14. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of suvorexant or other dual orexin receptor antagonists over no dual orexin receptor antagonists (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 15. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests against the use of triazolam and other benzodiazepines (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation: 16. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty).

Remark

For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 17. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night and fixed daytime sleep timing over the combination of no bright light and no fixed sleep timing (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 18. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night, fixed daytime sleep timing, and reduced-light-transmittance glasses in the morning over the combination of no bright light, no fixed sleep timing, and no reduced-light-transmittance glasses (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark 1 : For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. Remark 2: Attention to driving safety is important when wearing reduced-light-transmittance glasses. Other considerations for adults with SWD: 19. In adults with SWD who are working either an 8-hour or 12-hour night shift, the AASM does not suggest working one shift duration over the other (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).

Remark

This recommendation does not consider other shift durations, rotation, or the number of consecutive shifts. This guideline did not look at shift durations exceeding 12 hours. The total number of hours worked per week ranged from 36 to 52.
