raw.abstractText:
Background

High-grade (HG) bladder urothelial carcinoma is an aggressive tumor with poor outcomes, underscoring the need for early molecular stratification. However, a comprehensive functional understanding of its metabolic landscape remains limited. This study aims to delineate the proteomic and metabolic hallmarks of HG bladder cancer by leveraging formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue archives.

Methods

We performed integrated proteomic (data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry) and untargeted metabolomic profiling on FFPE specimens from a discovery cohort of 56 patients (27 low-grade/LG, 29 HG). Key findings were validated via immunohistochemistry (IHC) on an independent cohort of 60 patients (30 LG, 30 HG).

Results

Proteomics revealed extensive molecular remodeling in HG tumors, with 2,506 differentially expressed proteins enriched in metabolic pathways. Metabolomics identified 67 altered metabolites, highlighting a profoundly rewired metabolic network. Integrated analysis converged on 2 core pathways: (1) enhanced nucleotide anabolism supported by the upregulation of enzymes including phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), and (2) a collapsed creatine-phosphagen system evidenced by marked decreases in creatine/creatinine. IHC validation confirmed significant upregulation of PHGDH in HG tumors. Intriguingly, while metabolomic and DIA‑MS‑based proteomic data indicated downregulation of guanidinoacetate N‑methyltransferase (GAMT), the terminal enzyme for creatine biosynthesis, IHC on an independent validation cohort demonstrated robust GAMT immunoreactive accumulation within HG tumor cells. This multi‑omics discordance points toward complex, non‑canonical dysregulation consistent with a working model of protein‑catalytic‑function decoupling, which is presented as a testable working model requiring further experimental validation.

Conclusion

This multi-omics study defines a metabolic dichotomy in HG bladder cancer, characterized by concurrent anabolic reinforcement and energy buffer collapse. We validate PHGDH as a consistent biomarker and uncover complex dysregulation of GAMT, consistent with a testable working model involving putative post-translational modifications, protein truncation, aberrant subcellular sequestration, or gain-of-non-canonical functions. Our findings provide novel metabolic biomarkers and reveal an unexpected layer of complexity in the molecular pathology of advanced bladder cancer.

raw.abstractText: GABA is a neurotransmitter and a four-carbon non-protein amino acid that is produced from L-glutamate through an enzymatic decarboxylation reaction catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase (GAD). This amino acid is naturally present in microorganisms, plants, and animals. As a neurotransmitter in the central nervous system of mammals, GABA plays a pivotal role in regulating neuronal excitability and maintaining the balance of neural activity. Growing interest in improving human health and developing functional foods has increased global attention toward GABA, leading to considerable interest in its incorporation and enrichment in food products. Despite the potential health benefits of GABA, endogenous GABA concentrations in many food matrices are relatively low, limiting their potential as dietary sources. Consequently, enrichment strategies, including fermentation, germination, and other bioprocessing approaches, have attracted attention as alternatives to direct GABA addition and may facilitate the development of GABA-enriched functional foods. Overall, this review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding GABA biosynthesis, its physiological functions, and its applications in food products. It also discusses current strategies for GABA enrichment and highlights the factors influencing its production and applications.

payload.title: Micronutrient deficiencies in continuous renal replacement therapy: A literature review and the emerging role of the pharmacist.
payload.abstract: Evaluating micronutrient deficiencies in the critically ill population is challenging given the complex clinical picture for many patients. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is a risk factor for micronutrient deficiencies in this cohort, with deficiencies resulting from increased losses in dialysis effluent or adsorption to tubing or to the dialysis filter. The aim of this article is to summarize pertinent research literature regarding micronutrient supplementation and monitoring in CRRT and identify areas for pharmacists to improve patient outcomes from a nutrition standpoint. A computerized literature search was conducted of the PubMed electronic database, and articles were included if they discussed one of the prespecified micronutrients and renal replacement therapy. The micronutrients specifically addressed in this article are copper, selenium, zinc, L-carnitine, vitamin C, vitamin B1, vitamin B6, and vitamin B9. For each of these micronutrients, we summarize the evidence for deficiencies in CRRT and supplementation strategies. However, in many cases, literature is lacking to support supplementation and monitoring strategies specifically in CRRT. Current literature recognizes that standard supplementation may not be enough in the critically ill population on CRRT, but evidence is lacking for optimal micronutrient supplementation doses and monitoring parameters. Until future literature is available, pharmacists should be aware of these deficiencies and help guide recommendations for supplementation.

payload.title: Anti-GABA B receptor autoimmunity causes cognitive decline by presynaptic pathology
payload.abstract: The GABA B receptor is a central regulator of neuronal transmission and excitability by pre- and postsynaptic mechanisms. Its dysfunction causes severe neurological disease, but the underlying pathomechanisms remain elusive. Here, we exploit a distinct CNS autoimmune disorder in which patients develop specific autoantibodies against GABA B receptors causing autoimmune encephalitis with severe memory dysfunction and epilepsy. We demonstrate that human autoantibodies target the sushi-domains of the GABA B receptor B1a subunit and the B2 subunit and interfere with presynaptic signaling. This specific presynaptic pathology results from exclusive functional antagonism of the B1a subunit and disrupts short- and long-term synaptic plasticity, abnormally amplifies hippocampal network oscillations and coupling in vivo, and ultimately impairs memory consolidation. Our results demonstrate that autoimmune presynaptic pathomechanisms alone are sufficient to interfere with memory processing, thus defining a causal link between molecular GABA B receptor disturbance, synaptic pathology, circuit dysfunction, and dementia distinct from classical neurodegenerative processes.
